desc: This station involves taking a focussed pre-immunosuppression risk history and counselling a young man with Crohn's disease about a positive hepatitis B screening result, faecal calprotectin and the choice of advanced therapy.
explain:
Pre-treatment screening for advanced IBD therapy

Before anti-TNF therapy, screen for latent TB (IGRA and/or tuberculin skin test, with a risk and symptom history and chest imaging as indicated), hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), hepatitis C, HIV and varicella immunity. TNF blockade can reactivate latent TB and hepatitis B, causing disseminated or severe disease. In this case the IGRA is negative, but HBsAg and anti-HBc positivity with negative anti-HBs indicates chronic hepatitis B infection.

Managing hepatitis B before immunosuppression

Chronic hepatitis B needs HBV DNA, HBeAg, liver function tests and fibrosis assessment, ideally with hepatology or gastroenterology input. Antiviral prophylaxis (tenofovir or entecavir) is started before immunosuppression and continued during and for a period afterwards, as advised by the specialist. The biologic is started once antiviral therapy is in place; this is a short delay rather than a refusal of treatment.

Hepatitis B and hepatocellular carcinoma

Chronic hepatitis B causes hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which can occur even without cirrhosis. Prevention relies on vaccination (starting with a birth dose, with HBIG for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers) and, for people already infected, linkage to care and antivirals when indicated. In Australia, six-monthly HCC ultrasound surveillance is recommended for people with cirrhosis and for non-cirrhotic people with chronic hepatitis B in higher-risk groups, which includes Asian-born men aged 40 years or older and those with a family history of HCC. At 29, without cirrhosis or a family history of HCC, Mr Nguyen may not need surveillance yet, and the decision depends on his fibrosis or cirrhosis status, family history and age. A candidate should not promise him 6-monthly ultrasounds now.

Faecal calprotectin

Faecal calprotectin is a stool marker of neutrophil-driven intestinal inflammation. In adults with chronic lower bowel symptoms where cancer is not suspected (red flags need urgent investigation), a low result makes IBD unlikely, a raised result prompts gastroenterology referral, and a borderline result is repeated per local pathway. In known IBD it is used for non-invasive monitoring of disease activity between colonoscopies.

Vedolizumab

Vedolizumab is an anti-alpha4beta7 integrin antibody that blocks lymphocyte trafficking to the gut. It is gut-selective with a favourable safety profile, but has a slower onset of action than anti-TNF agents. It does not remove the need for a hepatitis B plan.
focus: Counselling before starting advanced therapy for IBD
guide:
A high-performing candidate takes a brief, targeted history that covers hepatitis B risk factors (country of birth, maternal infection, vaccination, partner) and TB and vaccine status. They then explain clearly and sensitively that he has chronic hepatitis B, why that matters before anti-TNF therapy (reactivation), and that the biologic will not be started until antiviral therapy is in place. They answer his questions about calprotectin (diagnostic and monitoring use), vedolizumab (gut-selective, favourable safety, slower onset), and liver cancer risk, without over- or under-promising surveillance. They end with a safe plan, contact tracing and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes an unfocussed history, uses jargon, or reports the result without explaining why it affects treatment. They may say that he will definitely need 6-monthly ultrasounds, may omit the antiviral plan, or may not link hepatitis B to liver cancer. They may state that he cannot have biologic therapy at all, leaving the patient distressed, and may overlook his partner.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Minh Nguyen.

  • Age: 29-years-old.

  • Gender: Male (he/him).

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No.

  • Setting: General practice clinic. You are anxious and slightly worried about what the 'abnormal' test means.

Opening statement: "The nurse said one of my tests was abnormal. Is it serious? I just want to get my bowel sorted."

History if asked (2 minutes):

  • Crohn's disease: Diarrhoea 5-6 times per day with some blood, cramping right-sided abdominal pain and tiredness for 6 weeks. Weight has dropped about 2 kg. Currently on azathioprine and finishing a prednisolone taper.

  • Hepatitis B risk factors: Born in Vietnam and moved to Australia aged 12. Your mother has hepatitis B and sees a liver specialist. You do not know whether you were ever vaccinated. No history of injecting drugs, no tattoos or piercings, no blood transfusions. One long-term partner (Linh) for 3 years, who has not been tested; you use condoms inconsistently. Alcohol: 2 standard drinks per week. No family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis. You have never had a liver problem diagnosed.

  • TB risk and symptoms: You have a BCG scar from childhood. Visited Vietnam for 3 weeks about 2 years ago. No known TB contacts. No cough, fevers or night sweats (other than the weight loss attributed to the bowel flare). No previous chest X-ray.

  • Immunity and vaccines: Had chickenpox as a child. No live vaccines recently. No other regular medications. No allergies.

If asked about your understanding: "I didn't know I had hepatitis B. I feel fine apart from my bowel."

Reactions during counselling:

  • When told of the hepatitis B result, appear worried: "Did I catch it from Linh? Is she at risk?"

  • If the candidate says you will not be able to start the biologic at all, become upset: "So I'm stuck with this bowel for ever?" Settle if the candidate explains that treatment will be started once the antiviral is in place.

  • Interrupt the candidate if they use medical jargon (for example 'seroconversion', 'reactivation', 'integrin', 'prophylaxis') without a plain explanation, saying: "Sorry, what does that mean?"

If the candidate has not already addressed these by about 5 minutes into the station, ask the following questions:

  1. "Why do I keep having to do poo tests? What is the calprotectin one for, and does it mean I definitely have Crohn's?"

  2. "Why can't I just start the injection now?"

  3. "Is there a gentler option for my immune system?"

  4. "Am I going to get liver cancer? Do I need scans?"

The candidate may ask further questions of you; use only the provided history above. The candidate should use non-medical terminology.
points: Before anti-TNF therapy, screen for latent TB, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and varicella immunity, because TNF blockade can reactivate TB and hepatitis B.
Chronic hepatitis B needs antiviral prophylaxis before immunosuppression; delay the biologic until it is in place.

Chronic hepatitis B causes HCC, even without cirrhosis; prevent with vaccination from birth and HBIG for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers. HCC surveillance depends on cirrhosis, family history and age (not automatic at 29).
Faecal calprotectin helps decide who needs colonoscopy or referral when IBD is suspected (low makes IBD unlikely) and monitors activity in known IBD.
Vedolizumab is gut-selective with a favourable safety profile but a slower onset of action.

stem:
You are a general practice registrar. Minh Nguyen is a 29-year-old man with ileocolonic Crohn's disease diagnosed 18 months ago. He has had a moderate-to-severe flare despite azathioprine and a recent prednisolone course. A gastroenterologist has recommended starting advanced therapy and has asked you to complete the pre-treatment screening bloods. He is likely to be offered an anti-TNF agent (for example infliximab or adalimumab), and vedolizumab is also being considered.

Results of the screening bloods are now back:

  • Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA): negative.

  • Hepatitis B: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc (total) positive, anti-HBs negative.

  • Hepatitis C antibody and HIV: negative.

  • Varicella IgG: immune.

  • ALT: mildly elevated at 52 U/L. Hepatitis B DNA and HBeAg have been requested and are pending.

  • Faecal calprotectin (taken at the time of the flare): 640 mcg/g.

The practice nurse has told Mr Nguyen that one blood test was abnormal and that he needs to discuss it with you. He has not yet been told what it means.

For the purpose of this station, assume that the results above are correct and that the gastroenterology team is happy for you to begin the work-up and discuss options with him.
tasks: Take a focussed pre-immunosuppression risk history, including risk factors for the abnormal result (2 minutes).
Counsel Mr Nguyen about his results and the next steps before advanced therapy (6 minutes).
title: Pre-biologic screening: an abnormal hepatitis B result in Crohn's disease
